140.0.0.en: Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man; which imagine mischiefs in their heart; continually are they gathered together for war.

140.0.1.en: 1- David asks God to deliver him from the wicked and the unjust, especially since they may not show their evil at first, or may be hypocrites who show the opposite of what is within them, but they certainly think evil in their hearts. This evil appears in wronging others and fighting them, so David asks God to deliver him before the evil happens. This shows David's need and humility, in addition to the evil surrounding him and his need for help from God, and it certainly shows his strong faith in the power of God.

140.0.2.en: 2- The wicked are the demons and all who follow them among men. These are selfish people who think only of themselves and wrong others, but they unite only in evil, gathering to fight the righteous and wrong them, yet the power of God is able to deliver the righteous, even if all the demons gather against them.

140.1.0.en: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah.

140.1.1.en: Adder (al-ufu'an): the male of the venomous snake.

140.1.2.en: Poison (hummah): the venom of a snake or scorpion.

140.1.3.en: 1- David likens these wicked people in their cunning and evil to the serpent, which keeps its venom, so they keep the venom under their tongues and lips; that is, the tongues of these wicked people are harsh and sharp and want to kill whoever meets them. The Apostle Paul repeated this verse to show the evil of the wicked (Rom 3:13).

140.1.4.en: 2- These wicked people whose tongues kill others are the heretics and the malicious servants who proclaim any teachings foreign to the mind of God and of the Church.

140.1.5.en: 3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause, so that the psalmist may reflect on this psalm, guard against the wicked, and ask for God's help. The word Selah is repeated three times in this psalm. It appeared often in the first part of the Psalms, but in the last part, in which we now are, this is the first time.

140.2.0.en: Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the violent man; who have purposed to overthrow my goings. The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah. Overthrow my goings: they make me fall into a stumbling, that is, they make me fall into sin and keep me away from God.

140.2.1.en: Gins (ashrak): plural of sharak, which is a trap or snare.

140.2.2.en: 1- Here he appeals to God in a supplicating prayer to deliver him from the wicked and violent man who think of making him fall, using all cunning and malice, which he likens to the cunning of the hunter who uses snares, cords, nets and traps. This shows the variety of the warfare of the devil and of the wicked who surround David, since Saul made various attempts to seize David and destroy him, but God delivered him from his hand.

140.2.3.en: 2- Nets and snares are set beside the way; if the righteous man walks in the way of God, nothing makes him stumble, but if he turns aside from the way, he falls into the hand of Satan.

140.2.4.en: 3- The Way is Christ, as He said of Himself (Jn 14:6), and He is humble and wants His children to be humble like Him. But the demons are the proud, so if the righteous walk humbly in the way of God, the demons are unable to fight them.

140.2.5.en: 4- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the importance of prayer, which delivers us from all the snares of the demons.

140.2.6.en: Hold fast to God's commandments, and remain in the Church and her sacraments with humility, and Satan will be unable to fight you.

140.3.0.en: I said unto the LORD, Thou art my God: hear the voice of my supplications, O LORD. O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.

140.3.1.en: 1- Before the various snares of the demons David was not disturbed, but looked to God and felt his boldness before Him, so he said to Him, You are my God. He made supplication to Him, that is, he asked Him with humility, and he even attributed power to Him, saying to Him, the strength of my salvation. All this made him calm and encouraged, and increased his clinging to God.

140.3.2.en: 2- He thanked God, who covered him in the day of battle. The covering here is the protection of his head from the arrows of enemies; that is, God became to him like a helmet protecting him from the wars of the wicked, and consequently David advanced and was victorious over the enemies, because God protects him; that is, David recalled his experience with God by thanking Him, so he was reassured and became strong. The helmet of salvation is affirmed to us by the Apostle Paul (1 Thess 5:8). And God covered His people in the wilderness of Sinai with the pillar of cloud, that is, He protected them from the scorching sun in the wilderness, as He now protects us from the temptations of the devil.

140.4.0.en: Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; further not his wicked device; lest they exalt themselves. Selah.

140.4.1.en: 1- David asks God not to give the wicked man his desire, that is, the destruction of David, but to bring to nothing his evil purposes of harming the righteous, and to show the emptiness of his pride and exaltation and his hatred of the righteous. By this He gives the wicked man an opportunity to review himself and repent, and at the same time He confirms the faith of the righteous in God.

140.4.2.en: 2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for reflection on the emptiness of evil and the power of God that brings his evil to nothing, and this through prayer.

140.5.0.en: As for the head of those that compass me about, let the mischief of their own lips cover them.

140.5.1.en: 1- The wicked spoke with deceitful and false lips in order to destroy the righteous man, but God intervened and turned their evils upon their own heads. The misery they wished with their lips for the righteous man turned back upon them and harmed them. Thus the venom under their lips mentioned in (v. 3) appeared upon their heads; that is, God openly showed their cunning and evil before the people. This is what happened with Saul, who pursued David, for he fell twice into David's hand, but David forgave him; and the brothers of Joseph sold him as a slave, and they became slaves to him; and Absalom tried to kill his father David and rose against him with a great army, and Absalom died a shameful death.

140.5.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom Satan rose up, and He was nailed to the Cross and died, and by His death He paid the debt on our behalf and bound Satan.

140.6.0.en: Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again. Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him.

140.6.2.en: David continues his explanation of what will happen to the wicked, saying that fire will fall upon them from heaven and they will perish, as happened to the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, and likewise to the murmurers who followed Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Num 16:32), and this fire that burns them leads them to the eternal fire. And he describes what happens to them as being drowned in water and perishing, as happened to Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, and as happened to the wicked in the Flood. All this happens to the wicked man of harsh tongue and to the unjust man, whose injustice leads him and makes him fall into destruction.

140.7.0.en: I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor. Surely the righteous shall give thanks unto thy name: the upright shall dwell in thy presence.

140.7.1.en: 1- If the wicked, as appeared in the preceding verses, will suffer pains resulting from their evils, being tormented as by fire and drowning waters, then on the contrary God, the Controller of all, cares for the poor and the afflicted, that is, the humble who have relied on Him, and He gives them just judgments, that is, He rewards them with peace in their hearts, so that they praise God and dwell in His presence, that is, they enjoy His company and rejoice; all this on earth.

140.7.2.en: 2- If the end of the wicked is eternal torment, then God the just Judge executes a just judgment for the poor and afflicted, and rewards them with the Kingdom of Heaven, where they continue their praise and thanksgiving to God forever, and enjoy sitting in His hands in His Kingdom.

140.7.3.en: Look at the glories that God has prepared for you so that you may endure the sufferings of the earth, and do not be dazzled by the temporary success of the wicked, for it will come upon their own heads. Only hold fast to your faith and know that God supports you and will never leave you.

140.7.4.en: The Lord keeps and delivers His children "LORD, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee" v. 1 Introduction:

140.7.5.en: 1- Its author: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.

140.7.6.en: 2- When it was written: during Saul's pursuit of David.

140.7.7.en: 3- It suits every person who wants to live with God and keep away from evil, who faces tests and temptations, and who is preparing for his eternity.

140.7.8.en: 4- This psalm is liturgical; it was prayed in the evening at the offering of the evening burnt offering.

140.7.9.en: 5- It is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, because at the end of the day a person reviews himself and asks God to keep him from evil and deliver him.

141.0.s.en: (1) A cry to be kept from evil

141.0.0.en: LORD, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee.

141.0.1.en: 1- David cries to God and asks Him to hear him attentively, and even to hasten to his help, and this shows:

141.0.2.en: a - his severe distress, and his urgent need of God's intervention.

141.0.3.en: b - David's boldness before God, and his sonship to Him, so he says, make haste and give ear.

141.0.4.en: c - his continuing to cry out, and consequently his constant need that God hear him. This is what happens in the life of believers in the Old Testament and in the Church of the New Testament.

141.0.5.en: 2- Crying out means prayer not only with the lips, but with the mind and all the feelings of the heart, and sometimes the cry is from within a person and is not accompanied by words from outside, as Moses did when he was before the Red Sea with Pharaoh's army behind him (Ex 14:15).

141.1.0.en: Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.

141.1.1.en: 1- David offers his prayer and wishes that it be like the incense that burns before God, giving off a sweet fragrance that pleases God. And he likens the lifting up of his hands to the evening sacrifice, which is the burnt offering that the Jews offered every evening on the bronze altar to please God. The hands always signify works, and lifting them before God means offering the good works that David did throughout the day, and he offers them to God.

141.1.2.en: 2- He mentioned incense before the sacrifice, because incense is offered in the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, while the sacrifice is offered on the bronze altar outside the Holy Place. The evening sacrifice is burned entirely before God, so that God may smell a sweet savor, and likewise the incense is burned entirely before the Holy of Holies to satisfy divine justice.

141.1.3.en: 3- Incense is placed on burning coals so that it burns and gives off its sweet fragrance; so also the heart, if it is kindled with the love of God, is inclined to give and sacrifice in order to please God, and its prayers are fervent and rise quickly to heaven.

141.1.4.en: 4- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who offered Himself at evening time on the Cross, and lifted His hands nailed to the Cross, and died for us; He is the burnt offering offered by the High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, He offered Himself on the Cross, and ascended as the fragrance of incense, and His good Father smelled it at evening time on Golgotha (the Sunday Midnight Praise).

141.1.5.en: 5- In the Church of the New Testament the priests offer the true sacrifice on the altar, which is the Body and Blood of the Lord. But all believers are also priests in the general sense of the priesthood, and not in the particular sense of the priest, the steward of God for the completion of the sacraments, for every believer offers his prayers, his praises, his service and all his good works as a sacrifice and incense before God every day.

141.2.0.en: Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.

141.2.1.en: 1- The tongue is a very important member of the body, for from it comes the speech that expresses the person, whether in good things or in evil; therefore David asks God to keep his mouth and his lips, which stand before the tongue like a door, for they represent the control of the tongue, and the Apostle James affirms the seriousness of the tongue (Jas 3).

141.2.2.en: 2- David asks for a watch for his mouth, that is, an external warning so that the tongue may not err, such as the occurrence of some event that stops speech, or the interruption of another person... He also asks for the keeping of his words, that is, an inner control from the person, so that he is careful and does not speak evil.

141.2.3.en: 3- David asks God for a watch and keeping of his tongue, so that he may speak what pleases God and be silent from evil speech, in addition to his silence for the sake of conversation with God, and so that he may listen to others and understand them, and ask for God's guidance and speak what he is permitted.

141.3.0.en: Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties.

141.3.1.en: 1- After asking for the control of his tongue, David moves on to the source of blessings or of evil, which is the inner heart, and he asks God not to allow his heart to incline to evil, but to incline always to good, and consequently his tongue will speak good things. For what is asked is not merely the control of the tongue while the heart is left to incline to evil, because the evil would then be suppressed within the person and would later burst out and appear; rather what is asked is the purifying of the heart, so that good speech comes out spontaneously (Lk 6:45).

141.3.2.en: 2- David also asked that his heart not persist in evil and support its evil with corrupt thoughts, and that he not agree with the workers of iniquity in their evils, nor mingle with them so as to sit in their assemblies and eat of their dainties, that is, their delicious foods that could arouse his desires, in addition to their evil words and deeds; what is meant is excessive mingling with the wicked, and consequently being affected by their conduct. In sum, he asks for his restraint with the wicked and for his not sharing in their evil deeds.

141.3.3.en: Remember that your goal in life is to be with God and praise Him, and to offer your life as a sacrifice of love for God and care for others. Do not share with the wicked in their evils, but keep your heart and your tongue in purity for God's sake.

141.4.s.en: (2) The salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked

141.4.0.en: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.

141.4.1.en: Shall not break (la ya'ba): does not refuse, that is, accepts.

141.4.2.en: 1- So that David may keep the purity of his heart and tongue, he accepts not only the direct chastisements of God, but also the chastisements and blows of the righteous, that is, the just. He considers this a mercy to him, for it keeps him from evil.

141.4.3.en: And the reproofs of the righteous prick him so that he does not fall into sin, and he even regards them as oil that anoints his head; for the ancients, when receiving their guests at banquets, used to anoint their heads with perfumed oil, so David regards the reproof of the righteous as perfumed oil on his head, which he accepts, because it will heal him of his sins, just as he accepted the reproof of Nathan the prophet for his sin; and out of David's love for the righteous he prays for them if calamities come upon them.

141.4.4.en: 2- In the Septuagint translation it says, "let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head"; on the other hand, David does not accept the oil with which sinners anoint him, since the sinners' care for him is hypocrisy. David prays that God may deliver him from their calamities, that is, their hypocrisy, and he prays that the sinners may take heed and repent and return to God, as he used to pray for his son Absalom, the hypocrite who sought to take the kingdom from him and drive him out.

141.5.0.en: When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet.

141.5.1.en: 1- The overthrow of the judges of the wicked, that is, their great ones, from the rock: this is what happened to Saul and the great ones of his army, for they were killed in the war with the Philistines. But David did not kill Saul when he fell into his hands, but reproached him with sweet words that carried love and submission, and also after Saul's death he cared for his offspring, Mephibosheth, and this love is regarded as sweet words.

141.5.2.en: 2- The judges, that is, the great ones of the proud wicked, were overthrown because of their pride, while the humble, such as David, God granted sweet words, and he was exalted and sat on the throne of the kingdom.

141.5.3.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, when the great ones of the world, of the Jews and the Gentiles, rose up against Him and crucified Him, and fell into a great sin, and collided with the Rock, who is Christ, and Satan himself, who moved them, was bound by Christ with the Cross. This verse also applies to the heretics who resisted the teachings of Christ, so they fell under His judgment, and in the Septuagint translation it says that these great ones "were swallowed up near the rock," that is, Christ drew them and others, and they believed in Him, as happened with Saul of Tarsus, that is, the Apostle Paul.

141.6.0.en: Our bones are scattered at the grave's mouth, as when one cutteth and cleaveth wood upon the earth.

141.6.1.en: David likens what happened to him and his men when they fled before Saul to the earth that is scattered when the farmer breaks up the ground with the plow; so also the souls of David's men were scattered at the mouth of Hades, that is, they came near to death from the severity of the hunger, thirst and exhaustion they suffered as a result of running and fleeing. He expresses the severe suffering he endured in the face of Saul's pursuit.

141.7.0.en: But mine eyes are unto thee, O GOD the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute. Keep me from the snare which they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity. Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape. Gins (ashrak): plural of sharak, that is, a snare or trap.

141.7.1.en: 1- David concludes the psalm with hope in God, to whom he lifted his eyes with humility, so that He may protect him from the wicked, and not leave his soul destitute, that is, leave him to perish, or that his soul be emptied of faith and courage, so that he becomes weak and goes away from God.

141.7.2.en: 2- He also asks God to keep him from the snares of the wicked that seek his destruction, but on the contrary let the sinners fall into their own nets and snares, while David alone escapes completely, and this is what happened, for Saul and his sons died in the war, and David escaped and reigned over the children of Israel.

141.7.3.en: 3- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane to the Father, and the Jews set up the Cross for Him as a snare and killed Him, but He escaped by His Resurrection, while they perished in AD 70 at the hand of Titus the Roman, who destroyed Jerusalem and killed a vast number of Jews.

141.7.4.en: If you humble yourself and accept God's chastisement and the reproof of those who love you, God will deliver you from every evil, whatever the plots of the wicked, and they will come upon their own heads, while you remain in your peace.

141.7.5.en: God who delivers from trouble A maschil of David, when he was in the cave: "A prayer"

141.7.6.en: "I cried unto the LORD with my voice; with my voice unto the LORD did I make my supplication" (v. 1) Introduction:

141.7.7.en: 1- Its author: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the psalm.

141.7.8.en: 2- When was it written? When David was pursued by King Saul and was in the cave, which was either the cave of Adullam (1 Sam 22) or the cave of Engedi (1 Sam 24). In both cases he was fleeing before Saul, and with David were a number of people persecuted by Saul and fleeing in the wilderness.

141.7.9.en: 3- There is a similarity between this psalm and Ps 57, for in both David was in the cave, as appears from their titles. But in (Ps 57) David appears strong and victorious by the power of God, while in this psalm David appears weak, taking refuge in God to deliver him from his enemies.

141.7.10.en: 4- This psalm suits every one who prays who suffers troubles and persecutions, yet has faith and hope in God, so he prays to Him and asks for His help.

141.7.11.en: 5- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of Christ persecuted by the Jews even to death.

141.7.12.en: 6- This psalm is also a prophecy about the Church persecuted throughout the ages, yet her refuge and portion is God.

141.7.13.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, where a person takes refuge in God at the end of the day and casts all his problems and troubles with confidence upon God, so that he may sleep in rest and have hope for the days that follow.
